cover.headline: Xior: full buildings, a heavy balance sheet
cover.notice: Prices are as of the close on 26 November 2026. Company figures come from the nine-month results published on 23 October 2026, the half-year results of 6 August 2026 and, for the split by country, the nine-month 2025 presentation. Yields, multiples, market value and the discount to net asset value are Syz calculations. This note is not a recommendation for any individual investor.
cover.h2: Student housing: a shortage the market will not pay for

left.p: Purpose-built student housing, residences let by the room or studio with services, is one of the few corners of European real estate where demand clearly exceeds supply. On the continent most students still live with their parents, in university halls or in small private flats; the share in professionally run beds is far below the UK level. Student numbers keep rising, international enrolment most of all, while new supply is held back by building costs, slow planning and expensive financing. Industry estimates put new deliveries at about 2% of the stock a year, short of growth in international students.

This shows in the operating numbers. In the better university cities buildings are close to full and rents have risen faster than inflation for several years: Xior, the only listed specialist on the continent, reported 98.5% occupancy at the end of September and like-for-like rental growth of 4.62%. Demand also holds up in downturns, when enrolment tends to rise.

left.sub2: The struggle is on the financing side

left.p: Strong operations have not protected valuations or share prices. Student housing is a long-lived, low-yielding asset financed partly with debt, so it is a bet on interest rates as much as on rents. When rates rose in 2022 and 2023, valuers raised the yields they apply to rents, values fell and leverage ratios rose mechanically. Listed owners have traded well below net asset value since, which makes new shares a costly way to fund growth. Growth now has to come from rents, disposals and costs, not acquisitions.

right.p: Student rents are politically visible. In the Netherlands, one of Xior's two home markets, the Affordable Rent Act of July 2024 extended a points-based rent cap to a much larger part of the private market, and heavier taxes on rental property have pushed small landlords out. That deepens the shortage but caps what owners can charge. The government has also sought to slow the intake of international students into English-taught courses. Rent caps, taxes and visa rules can each cut into the growth that drives the case, and they change faster than a building can be repositioned.

Financing costs are the other slow-moving pressure. Debt raised before 2022 was cheap and largely hedged; as hedges and loans roll off, it is refinanced at higher rates, absorbing part of the rental growth. Xior's average cost of debt was about 3.05% in the first quarter, 89% hedged for an average of 4.6 years: manageable today, a drag in the years ahead.

The sector offers what few property segments can: full buildings, rents growing faster than inflation and a structural shortage. The price is a balance sheet sensitive to rates, and share prices that track bond yields more than rents. For listed exposure the debate is less about demand than about whether leverage can come down without selling assets cheaply or issuing shares far below asset value. Size is a further constraint: with about EUR 1.2bn of market value and EUR 1.4m traded a day, Xior is a small, thinly traded stock.

fiche.title: Xior Student Housing (XIOR BB)
fiche.subtitle: Record occupancy and a 7.2% yield, held back by leverage above its own 50% ceiling

left.p: Xior is a Belgian real estate investment trust, listed in Brussels since 2015, that owns and runs student housing in eight countries: Belgium, the Netherlands, Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany, Denmark and Sweden, with about 22,000 lettable units. The EUR 939m purchase of Basecamp in 2022 took it into Germany and the Nordics, and also lifted its debt.

Operations are at their best. Occupancy reached 98.5% at the end of September and like-for-like rents rose 4.62%; management expects at least 4.4% for the full year. Nine-month EPRA earnings, the recurring profit of a property company, rose 6% to EUR 74.0m. Guidance is EPRA earnings per share of EUR 2.30 for 2026 and EUR 2.40 for 2027, with dividends of EUR 1.84 and EUR 1.92 (80% payout). Property values have stabilised, up 0.95% since January on higher rents.

It is the only listed pure play on continental student housing, with scale in fragmented markets, locations close to universities and its own operating platform. A small active pipeline of EUR 171m means growth now comes mainly from rents in existing buildings.

right.p: On paper the share is cheap: 34% below EPRA net tangible assets, 11.1 times 2026 guided earnings and a 7.2% dividend yield covered by recurring profit. The discount is the market's verdict on leverage. Loan-to-value has risen every quarter this year, from 49.87% at the end of 2025 to 50.56% in June and 51.31% in September, despite higher valuations, mainly because about EUR 80m of dividends is paid in cash. Bringing it below 50% by December implies disposals or other measures in the fourth quarter. Issuing shares at a 34% discount would destroy value, so asset sales are the realistic route, and their price against book value will show whether the valuations hold.

Leverage above target, with rates staying high. Refinancing at higher cost as hedges expire. Rent regulation, mainly in the Netherlands (about a third of units), and curbs on international students. Disposals below book value. Size and liquidity: with a market value of about EUR 1.2bn and about EUR 1.4m of shares traded a day on average over three months, Xior is too small for many large funds, a sizeable order can move the price, and selling can take days in a stressed market. A change of finance chief during deleveraging: the CFO leaves at the end of 2026 and the successor, a former sell-side analyst, starts by 1 February 2027, subject to regulatory approval.
Loan-to-value at 31 December in the full-year results, expected in early February; the size and price of disposals; the cost of new debt; confirmation of 2027 guidance; the 2027/28 letting season.

fiche.conclusion: Xior is running its buildings better than at any time since 2019, and its recurring earnings and dividend keep growing by about 4% a year. The share price does not reflect that: it reflects a loan-to-value above management's own ceiling that has risen through 2026. The yield and the discount to asset value leave room for a re-rating if leverage comes down through disposals at or near book value and long-term rates stop rising. Until that is visible, the balance sheet rather than the rental market is likely to drive the shares.

geo.title: Where Xior's buildings are
geo.intro: Xior owns or is completing about 25,500 student units in 42 cities across eight countries. The Netherlands and Belgium, where the company started, still hold more than half of the units; Poland, Spain and Portugal, the markets management sees as most undersupplied, hold about a third. The split below counts units, including committed projects, at 30 September 2025, the latest breakdown the company has published; the split by value can differ, since rents and values per unit vary widely between cities.

reading.sub2: What the map means for an investor

reading.p: Concentration is in regulated markets. About 54% of units are in the Netherlands and Belgium. Dutch rent rules and student-intake policy therefore matter more to the earnings than any single growth market.

Growth is in the south and east. Poland, Spain and Portugal have far fewer purpose-built beds per student than north-western Europe, and Xior's recent openings, such as Warsaw in 2025, are there. These markets bring higher growth but also currency risk in Poland and less market depth if assets must be sold.

The 2022 Basecamp portfolio added Poland, Germany, Denmark and Sweden. Germany and Sweden are small positions of one or two cities, and are the kind of assets a company can sell when it needs to reduce debt.

glossary.title: A cheat sheet for the generalist
glossary.intro: Student housing companies are judged on a handful of property metrics that differ from those used for industrial or consumer companies. The table explains the main ones, why they matter and where Xior stands.
rows: Share of beds that are let.
Drives revenue. Beds are let once a year, for the academic year, so the summer letting season sets most of the next twelve months.
Rent growth on the same buildings, excluding purchases and sales.
Measures pricing power; the test is whether it beats inflation.
+4.62% year on year; at least 4.4% guided for 2026
Recurring profit: rents less costs, interest and tax, excluding property revaluations and hedging gains or losses.
The relevant earnings figure for a property company; reported net profit swings with valuations.
Share of EPRA earnings paid as dividend; dividend divided by the share price.
Belgian REITs must pay out most of their earnings, so the dividend is the main return. A payout near 100% leaves no cushion.
Net tangible assets: appraised property value less debt, excluding deferred tax and hedges.
The property company's book value, based on independent valuations.
Share price against NTA per share.
The market's view of the valuations, the debt and the growth. A deep discount makes new shares costly to issue.
Annual rent divided by the property's value, as used by valuers.
Small changes move values a lot: on a 5% yield, a rise of 0.25 point cuts values by about 5%.
Net debt divided by the value of the properties.
The key balance-sheet risk: the same debt on lower values gives a higher LTV.
Belgian legal measure of debt to total assets for REITs.
The legal ceiling is 65%; banks and investors want a wide margin below it.
Cost of debt and hedge ratio
Average interest rate paid; share of debt fixed or swapped, and for how long.
Shows how quickly higher market rates feed into earnings.
Purpose-built beds as a share of full-time students in a city or country.
A low rate signals room for new supply, and a shortage that supports rents.
Low on the continent against the UK
Adds future rent, but must be paid for with debt, equity or disposals.
Share price times shares; value of shares traded each day.
Small, thinly traded stocks are harder to buy or sell in size, and can be left out by large funds.
About EUR 1.2bn; about EUR 1.4m a day
